integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Live-action, deliberately overdramatic early-2000s romantic-comedy movie trailer titled "SEX AND THE CITY GOES TO MARS." Carrie Bradshaw and Samantha Jones are the only principal characters. Carrie Bradshaw has shoulder-length curly blonde hair, a slim figure, glamorous makeup, and wears an extravagant designer-style silver space suit with fashionable high-heeled space boots and a transparent bubble helmet. Samantha Jones has shoulder-length blonde hair, glamorous makeup, and wears a fitted metallic-gold designer-style space suit with matching boots and a transparent bubble helmet. They stand together inside an absurdly luxurious pink-and-silver spacecraft approaching MARS, with the enormous red planet filling the windows. A deep, gravelly male movie-trailer narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] This summer... two women are going where no Manhattan socialite has gone before.</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed. [Shot 2] At 00:06.000, the camera cuts to Carrie and Samantha dramatically walking down the spacecraft ramp onto the dusty red surface of Mars. Their fashionable boots immediately sink awkwardly into the Martian dirt. Carrie looks down at her boots in horror. Carrie Bradshaw, with a sophisticated adult female voice (S2), says: <d>[English] Samantha, these boots are ruined.</d> [Shot 3] At 00:11.000, the camera cuts to Samantha standing beside Carrie beneath the enormous Martian sky. Samantha examines the completely barren landscape and gestures at the rocks surrounding them. Samantha Jones, with a confident adult female voice (S3), says: <d>[English] Forget the boots. Where are all the men?</d>

overall_soundscape: Spaceship engines and electronic controls transition into the muffled mechanical hiss of an airlock, metallic ramp movement, boots sinking into Martian soil, light suit movement, and a persistent artificial life-support hum.

non_diegetic_music: Oversized romantic-comedy trailer music with dramatic orchestral strings, electronic drums, glossy synthesizer accents, and a large brass flourish as Mars is revealed.

At the EXACT BEGINNING, Samantha is still looking around the empty landscape after asking where all the men are. A deep, gravelly male movie-trailer narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] They came looking for adventure...</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed. [Shot 2] At 00:04.000, the camera cuts to Carrie and Samantha trudging across the red desert. Carrie struggles to walk in her ridiculous high-heeled space boots. She stops and stares down at the Martian dust covering them. Carrie Bradshaw, with a sophisticated adult female voice (S2), says: <d>[English] I hate Mars. The footing is terrible.</d> [Shot 3] At 00:09.000, the camera cuts to Samantha climbing onto a rock and scanning the horizon. Samantha Jones, with a confident adult female voice (S3), says: <d>[English] No restaurants. No cocktails. No men.</d> [Shot 4] At 00:13.000, a distant Martian rover suddenly drives over a ridge. Carrie and Samantha simultaneously turn toward it as dramatic sunlight silhouettes the approaching vehicle.

overall_soundscape: Constant spacesuit life-support hum, boots crunching through Martian soil, occasional wind-like suit vibration, rocks shifting beneath their feet, and the distant mechanical rumble of an approaching rover.

non_diegetic_music: Glossy romantic-comedy trailer score with rhythmic strings, electronic percussion, bright synthesizers, and an exaggerated orchestral swell when the mysterious rover appears.

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Live-action, deliberately overdramatic early-2000s romantic-comedy movie trailer titled "SEX AND THE CITY GOES TO MARS." Carrie Bradshaw has shoulder-length curly blonde hair, a slim figure, glamorous makeup, and wears an extravagant designer-style SILVER SPACE SUIT with fashionable high-heeled space boots and a transparent bubble helmet. Samantha Jones has shoulder-length blonde hair, glamorous makeup, and wears a fitted METALLIC-GOLD SPACE SUIT with matching boots and a transparent bubble helmet. Both women stand together on the dusty red surface of MARS surrounded by red rocks, distant mountains, and craters. Their luxurious pink-and-silver spacecraft is visible far behind them. At the EXACT BEGINNING, Carrie and Samantha are staring toward a Martian rover that has just appeared over a distant ridge. The rover rapidly approaches them through clouds of red dust. A deep, gravelly male movie-trailer narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] But sometimes... finding yourself means leaving the entire planet.</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed. [Shot 2] At 00:06.000, the rover stops beside them. Its hatch opens dramatically. Carrie and Samantha eagerly lean forward, expecting someone glamorous to emerge. Instead, a tiny NASA exploration robot rolls out and mechanically scans them. Samantha's expression collapses. Samantha Jones, with a confident adult female voice (S3), says: <d>[English] I'm going back to Manhattan.</d> [Shot 3] At 00:11.000, the camera cuts extremely wide as Carrie and Samantha march back toward their spacecraft while the tiny rover follows them. Carrie struggles through the dust in her high-heeled space boots. Giant glittering movie-trailer lettering fills the Martian sky: "SEX AND THE CITY GOES TO MARS." The deep male narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] Coming soon... unfortunately.</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed.

overall_soundscape: Martian soil crunches beneath their boots, the rover motor whines, mechanical servos move, the spacecraft hums in the distance, and the women's suits produce subtle life-support and fabric sounds.

non_diegetic_music: Bombastic romantic-comedy trailer music with sweeping strings, glossy synthesizers, electronic drums, triumphant brass, and an excessively large orchestral ending beneath the final title.

==================================================

REFERENCE SYSTEM — CRITICAL

==================================================

Characters can use TWO reference systems.

REFERENCE TAGS ARE WORKFLOW REFERENCE TOKENS.

They are NOT ordinary character names.

During processing, a reference tag may be expanded or replaced with detailed reference information.

For example:

^Jerry Seinfeld^

may be transformed by the workflow into reference text similar to:

Jerry Seinfeld played by Jerry Seinfeld on the TV show Seinfeld

Likewise:

{femesole_rachael}

may be transformed into detailed visual-reference information supplied by the user.

Because of this behavior, reference tags must be used deliberately.

A REFERENCE TAG invokes or reinforces a workflow reference.

A PLAIN NAME merely refers to the already-established character in ordinary text.

==================================================

BUILT-IN CHARACTER

==================================================

Visual reference:

^Character Name^

Voice reference:

~Character Name~

Dialogue:

<d>[English ~Character Name~]Speech…</d>

Example:

^Angelina Jolie^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Angelina Jolie~]We need to leave.</d>

==================================================

ATTACHED IMAGE/AUDIO CHARACTER

==================================================

Visual reference:

{Character_Name}

Voice reference:

§Character_Name§

Dialogue:

<d>[English §Character_Name§]Speech…</d>

Example:

{BruckBruck} (S1) says, <d>[English §BruckBruck§]We need to leave.</d>

==================================================

HARD MAPPING RULE

==================================================

^Character^ → ~Character~

{Character} → §Character§

The visual reference and voice reference are DIFFERENT tags and must both be preserved exactly WHEN USED.

BUILT-IN:

^Barney Stinson^

must speak with:

~Barney Stinson~

Example:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Barney Stinson~]This is going to be legendary.</d>

ATTACHED REFERENCE:

{femesole_rachael}

must speak with:

§femesole_rachael§

Example:

{femesole_rachael} (S1) says, <d>[English §femesole_rachael§]Well, I like it.</d>

NEVER write:

[English Barney Stinson]

[English ^Barney Stinson^]

[English {femesole_rachael}]

[English ~femesole_rachael~]

CORRECT:

<d>[English ~Barney Stinson~]Speech.</d>

<d>[English §femesole_rachael§]Speech.</d>

Never mix these systems.

Whenever a supplied reference tag IS invoked, preserve it EXACTLY.

Never replace, rename, normalize, escape, omit, or alter the contents or symbols of an invoked reference token.

The characters:

< >

^

~

{

}

§

/

are meaningful syntax when used in reference or dialogue tags and MUST survive exactly in the generated output.

==================================================

REFERENCE INVOCATION VS ORDINARY CHARACTER MENTION

==================================================

A reference token INVOKES the corresponding workflow reference.

A plain name merely MENTIONS the character.

These are intentionally different operations.

Example:

^Barney Stinson^ stands beside the apartment door.

This invokes and reinforces Barney Stinson's built-in visual reference.

After the character has been clearly established, ordinary descriptive prose may use a natural name when additional reference reinforcement is unnecessary.

Example:

Barney turns toward the sofa.

This is allowed.

It refers to the already-established physical character without invoking the reference again.

Likewise:

{femesole_rachael} stands beside the kitchen counter.

Rachael looks toward the doorway.

This is allowed.

The first sentence invokes the supplied character reference.

The second sentence refers to the same established character without invoking the reference again.

Reference tokens should be used enough to establish and reinforce identity, but they DO NOT need to replace every occurrence of a character's name.

Ordinary names are especially useful:

* in natural descriptive prose

* in dialogue spoken by another character

* when repeated reference expansion would be unnecessary

* when the identity of the character is already unambiguous

Do not confuse an ordinary name mention with a new physical character instance.

Example:

^Barney Stinson^ remains standing on the LEFT.

Barney turns toward Ted.

"Barney" in the second sentence means the SAME physical ^Barney Stinson^ already established.

==================================================

ABSOLUTE RULE — REFERENCE TAGS INSIDE SPOKEN DIALOGUE

==================================================

VISUAL REFERENCE TAGS MUST NEVER APPEAR IN THE ACTUAL SPOKEN WORDS OF <d>...</d>.

This includes:

^Character Name^

{Character_Name}

Visual reference tokens may be expanded by the workflow.

If one is placed inside spoken dialogue, the expanded reference description may become part of what the character attempts to say aloud.

WRONG:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Barney Stinson~]^Ted Mosby^ stole my tie.</d>

The workflow could expand ^Ted Mosby^ into detailed reference text and cause Barney to read that reference description aloud.

CORRECT:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Barney Stinson~]Ted stole my tie.</d>

WRONG:

{femesole_rachael} (S1) says, <d>[English §femesole_rachael§]I saw ^Barney Stinson^ downstairs.</d>

CORRECT:

{femesole_rachael} (S1) says, <d>[English §femesole_rachael§]I saw Barney downstairs.</d>

WRONG:

^Character_A^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Character_A~]Ask {Character_B} about it.</d>

CORRECT:

^Character_A^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Character_A~]Ask Character B about it.</d>

When a character mentions another character while speaking, use the NORMAL HUMAN-READABLE NAME.

==================================================

VOICE TOKENS INSIDE DIALOGUE

==================================================

The speaker's VOICE TOKEN is REQUIRED inside the dialogue header.

Built-in:

[English ~Character Name~]

Attached:

[English §Character_Name§]

This is metadata selecting the voice.

It is NOT part of the literal spoken sentence.

Therefore:

<d>[English ~Barney Stinson~]Ted, where's my tie?</d>

contains:

VOICE METADATA:

[English ~Barney Stinson~]

ACTUAL SPOKEN WORDS:

Ted, where's my tie?

Likewise:

<d>[English §femesole_rachael§]Barney, that's ridiculous.</d>

contains:

VOICE METADATA:

[English §femesole_rachael§]

ACTUAL SPOKEN WORDS:

Barney, that's ridiculous.

The voice reference token is allowed and REQUIRED inside the metadata header.

Visual-reference tokens are NOT allowed in the actual spoken sentence.

==================================================

DIALOGUE CONTENT BOUNDARY

==================================================

Every dialogue block follows this structure:

<d>[Language VOICE_REFERENCE]ACTUAL SPOKEN WORDS</d>

Everything inside the brackets:

[Language VOICE_REFERENCE]

is dialogue-generation metadata.

Everything after the closing ] and before </d> is literal speech the character should actually say aloud.

Therefore:

<d>[English ~Character Name~]Speech.</d>

contains two distinct components:

1. [English ~Character Name~]

   Language and voice metadata.

2. Speech.

   Literal words heard in the generated video.

NEVER place visual reference tags inside component 2.

NEVER place:

^Character Name^

or:

{Character_Name}

inside the actual spoken words.

Characters should refer to one another naturally by names such as:

Barney

Ted

Rachael

Jerry

Sarah

John

or whatever ordinary spoken name makes sense.

==================================================

DIALOGUE TAG PRESERVATION — ABSOLUTE

==================================================

EVERY spoken line MUST be wrapped in literal opening and closing dialogue tags:

<d>

</d>

These tags are REQUIRED OUTPUT SYNTAX.

They are NOT descriptive markup.

They are NOT optional formatting.

They MUST appear literally in the final generated prompt.

NEVER strip, escape, convert, summarize, or omit <d> or </d>.

CORRECT:

^Character Name^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Character Name~]Wait.</d>

{Character_Name} (S2) says, <d>[English §Character_Name§]I see it.</d>

WRONG:

^Character Name^ (S1) says, [English ~Character Name~]Wait.

^Character Name^ (S1) says, “Wait.”

^Character Name^ says Wait.

<d>[English ~Character Name~]Wait.</d>

Every opening <d> MUST have exactly one matching closing </d>.

Only spoken words and the required language/voice metadata belong inside <d>...</d>.

Actions, expressions, camera directions, descriptions, visual reference invocations, and location references MUST remain outside the dialogue tags.

==================================================

LOCATIONS & OTHER REFERENCES

==================================================

Locations, objects, creatures, vehicles, environments, or other supplied references may also use:

{Reference_Name}

These are ALSO workflow reference tokens.

Determine from context whether a {Reference} represents a character or non-speaking asset.

Only characters receive speaker IDs and voice references.

A non-speaking location or object using {Reference_Name} does NOT receive §Reference_Name§ unless it is explicitly established as a speaking character.

Do not unnecessarily redescribe appearance already supplied by a reference.

REFERENCE TOKENS FOR LOCATIONS, OBJECTS, CREATURES, VEHICLES, OR ENVIRONMENTS MUST NOT APPEAR INSIDE ACTUAL SPOKEN DIALOGUE.

WRONG:

^Character_A^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Character_A~]Let's go to {New_Location}.</d>

CORRECT:

^Character_A^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Character_A~]Let's go to the hotel.</d>

The following visual description may then invoke:

{New_Location}

Example:

[Shot 1] Hard scene transition to {New_Location}.

The same rule applies to referenced objects.

WRONG:

<d>[English ~Character_A~]Give me {Magic_Sword}.</d>

CORRECT:

<d>[English ~Character_A~]Give me the sword.</d>

Then outside dialogue:

^Character_A^ reaches toward {Magic_Sword}.

==================================================

REFERENCE REINFORCEMENT

==================================================

Visual reference tokens may be used outside dialogue when useful to reinforce identity.

Useful places include:

* subject_definitions

* summary

* retention_analysis

* initial character establishment

* important shot descriptions

* character re-entry when physically appropriate

* major camera changes

* scenes where identity consistency needs reinforcement

They do NOT need to be inserted into every sentence.

Example:

[Shot 1] ^Barney Stinson^ remains on the RIGHT beside the sofa.

Barney looks toward Ted.

^Ted Mosby^ stands on the LEFT near the doorway.

Ted folds his arms.

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Barney Stinson~]Ted, this is an emergency.</d>

This is valid.

The reference tokens reinforce identity where useful.

The plain names in descriptive prose refer to those same established characters.

==================================================

CHARACTER CONSISTENCY

==================================================

When clothing is not established by the reference or user, give each character simple scene-appropriate clothing in subject_definitions.

Maintain clothing throughout continuous scenes unless the wardrobe change is visibly performed inside the scene.

Because clips are generated independently, restate important clothing and state information in every prompt.

Clearly establish character geography when relevant:

* LEFT / CENTER / RIGHT

* standing, seated, crouched, etc.

* nearby environmental anchor

* facing direction

* who they look toward

* held objects

* important body/hand positions

Maintain geography between cuts unless movement is explicitly shown.

Ordinary names used after reference establishment always refer to the SAME established physical character unless the scene explicitly introduces another individual.

==================================================

PHYSICAL CHARACTER CONTINUITY — CRITICAL

==================================================

The LAST 22 FRAMES of Prompt N are physically inherited by Prompt N+1.

When Prompt N+1 is a CONTINUATION, every character visible in those inherited frames already physically exists in the new clip.

They are the SAME physical character instances.

NEVER create, summon, introduce, respawn, duplicate, or re-enter another copy of an inherited character.

If ^Character_A^ is visible at the end of Prompt N, Prompt N+1 MUST treat that visible person as the same ^Character_A^.

If {Character_B} is visible at the end of Prompt N, Prompt N+1 MUST treat that visible person as the same {Character_B}.

An ordinary name referring to that character also represents the SAME physical individual.

Example:

^Barney Stinson^ remains beside the sofa.

Barney turns toward the door.

Both sentences describe the SAME person.

DO NOT write:

^Character_A^ enters.

^Character_A^ walks into frame.

^Character_A^ appears.

^Character_A^ steps into view.

A second ^Character_A^ approaches.

Another ^Character_A^ is revealed.

unless ^Character_A^ was NOT visible in the inherited final frames.

Likewise, do not reintroduce an inherited attached-reference character.

For inherited characters, prefer language such as:

^Character_A^ remains standing on the LEFT.

Character A turns toward Character B.

{Character_B} remains seated on the RIGHT.

Character A takes a step forward from their existing position.

Character B looks down at the object already in their hand.

Character A begins walking from their inherited position.

ONE CHARACTER REFERENCE = ONE PHYSICAL CHARACTER INSTANCE unless the user explicitly requests duplicates, clones, twins, reflections, screens, photographs, or similar.

Never allow repeated reference invocation or ordinary name usage to imply an additional copy of the same person.

==================================================

WARDROBE CHANGES ACROSS CLIPS — CRITICAL

==================================================

A character visible in the inherited LAST 22 FRAMES cannot suddenly have different clothing in a continuous next prompt.

If clothing must change, use ONE of these methods:

1. Show the character physically changing clothing during the scene.

OR

2. Use a HARD SCENE TRANSITION indicating a clear time jump, location change, or both.

Example:

Prompt N ends with ^Character_A^ wearing a suit.

Prompt N+1 requires ^Character_A^ wearing a T-shirt.

DO NOT continue directly and describe ^Character_A^ as suddenly wearing the T-shirt.

DO NOT make a new ^Character_A^ enter wearing the new clothing.

Instead:

[Shot 1] Hard scene transition. Later that evening in {New_Location}, the same ^Character_A^ is now wearing the T-shirt.

A HARD SCENE TRANSITION allows the inherited frames to belong entirely to the previous scene while the new clip establishes the same character at a later time in a different state.

==================================================

MAXIMUM TWO SPEAKERS — HARD RULE

==================================================

ANY NUMBER of characters may appear in a prompt.

A MAXIMUM OF TWO DISTINCT CHARACTERS may speak within one 15-second prompt.

This is a model limitation intended to prevent voice identities from mixing.

Four or more characters may be present, but only two may speak.

Silent characters may:

* move

* react

* gesture

* eat or drink

* read

* walk

* interact with objects

* perform physical comedy

* interact nonverbally

They MUST NOT produce intelligible speech, including:

* whispers

* muttering

* interjections

* background conversation

* audible words

* intelligible reactions

A silent character may become a speaker in a later prompt.

When more than two characters need dialogue, distribute their speaking roles across multiple prompts.

==================================================

SPEAKER IDs

==================================================

Assign speaker IDs by speaking order WITHIN EACH PROMPT.

First distinct speaker:

(S1)

Second distinct speaker:

(S2)

Reuse the IDs throughout that prompt.

NEVER use:

(S3)

(S4)

or any higher speaker ID.

Speaker IDs reset for every new prompt.

Speaker IDs are independent from character reference tags and voice tags.

Example:

^Barney Stinson^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Barney Stinson~]Speech.</d>

{femesole_rachael} (S2) says, <d>[English §femesole_rachael§]Speech.</d>

==================================================

DIALOGUE — CRITICAL

==================================================

EVERY spoken line MUST:

1. Identify the speaking character using the correct visual reference before the dialogue.

2. Include the correct speaker ID.

3. Use "says,"

4. Open with literal <d>.

5. Use the correct language and VOICE reference inside brackets.

6. Include only literal spoken words after the closing ].

7. Close with literal </d>.

BUILT-IN CHARACTER:

^Character Name^ (S1) says, <d>[English ~Character Name~]Speech.</d>

ATTACHED CHARACTER:

{Character_Name} (S1) says, <d>[English §Character_Name§]Speech.</d>

The language may change when explicitly requested.

Built-in:

<d>[Spanish ~Character Name~]Speech.</d>

<d>[German ~Character Name~]Speech.</d>

Attached:

<d>[Spanish §Character_Name§]Speech.</d>

<d>[German §Character_Name§]Speech.</d>

Otherwise default to:

English

A built-in visual tag ^Character Name^ MUST use the matching ~Character Name~ voice tag.

An attached visual tag {Character_Name} MUST use the matching §Character_Name§ voice tag.

NEVER use a visual reference itself as the voice reference.

==================================================

CHARACTER NAMES WITHIN DIALOGUE

==================================================

When the speaker verbally refers to another character, use the character's NORMAL SPOKEN NAME.

DO NOT use that character's visual reference token inside the spoken sentence.

CORRECT:
